analysis.one_liner: Protects the Arctic Refuge coastal plain from drilling by designating it wilderness.
analysis.headline: The bill to designate about 1.56 million acres of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge as wilderness never got a vote; it died in committee when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make roughly 1,559,538 acres of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge in Alaska — the coastal plain that the 2017 tax law opened to oil and gas leasing — part of the National Wilderness Preservation System. Wilderness is the strongest land protection in U.S. law: it bars new roads, motorized use, and commercial development, which would permanently close the area to drilling. The bill was introduced by Sen. Edward Markey with 25 Senate cosponsors in February 2023 and never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If the bill had passed, the protected area would remain undeveloped: the coastal plain's habitat for caribou, polar bears, and migratory birds would stay intact, the Gwich'in people whose culture and subsistence depend on the caribou herd would keep their way of life protected, and the public would keep a wild landscape and avoid the climate emissions drilling would produce. Existing oil and gas leases in the area would be effectively voided, shifting costs onto the leaseholders.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Conservationists, the Gwich'in people, and public-lands users

how_it_helps.text: The bill designates approximately 1,559,538 acres of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge in Alaska as wilderness under the Wilderness Act, using the 2015 'Coastal Plain Proposed Wilderness' map.

Land in the National Wilderness Preservation System is closed to commercial development, new roads, and most motorized use, so the designation would permanently prevent oil and gas drilling in the coastal plain — the very area Congress opened to leasing in the 2017 tax law.

The coastal plain is the calving ground of the Porcupine caribou herd, which the Gwich'in people of Alaska and Canada rely on for subsistence, so keeping it undeveloped protects their food supply and culture.

analysis.who_pays: The oil and gas industry bears the cost: wilderness designation would permanently close the coastal plain to exploration and drilling, voiding the value of leases sold in the area. Alaska would forgo potential royalty and tax revenue, and drilling proponents argue consumers and the federal treasury would forgo domestic energy supply.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas drillers and Alaska's treasury

drawbacks.text: Wilderness designation is permanent — unlike a leasing pause, it cannot be revisited by a future Congress without another act — so it forecloses domestic oil and gas development that drilling supporters argued would produce energy, jobs, and federal and state revenue from a field estimated to hold significant reserves.

The designation covers the 1.56-million-acre coastal plain, but the bill does not compensate leaseholders for the leases the government already sold in the area, which would likely trigger litigation and potential taxpayer compensation claims.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The trade is a permanent, irreversible protection for a unique ecosystem and an indigenous subsistence economy against foregone oil revenue and domestic energy supply. Supporters and opponents genuinely disagree about the weight of each side, but the bill's structure is straightforward: it converts a zone Congress opened to drilling in 2017 into the nation's strongest protected-land status, and the cost falls almost entirely on one concentrated industry and Alaska's revenue expectations.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never considered it, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Markey introduced the bill on February 7, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
Twenty-five senators — 24 Democrats and 1 Independent — cosponsored the bill, roughly a quarter of the Senate.

The Senate action history shows no further action: no committee markup, no floor vote, and no House counterpart activity in the record, so the bill died at the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The oil and gas industry is better off because the bill died: the coastal plain remains open to drilling under the 2017 tax law and its leases remain in place. Conservation groups and the Gwich'in gained nothing, and the question simply resets for the next Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas drillers and Alaska leaseholders

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor was a Democrat or Independent — 24 of 48 Senate Democrats plus 1 of 4 Independents — and no Republican signed on; the bill sat in committee controlled by the majority party without a vote.

industries.note: Wilderness designation would permanently close the Arctic Refuge coastal plain to drilling, voiding lease value in an area Congress opened to leasing in 2017. The industry's ability to develop the reserve runs directly against preserving the habitat and subsistence resources the bill protects.

industries.industry: Alaska state government and Alaskan communities reliant on energy revenue
industries.note: The state would forgo potential royalties, taxes, and jobs from coastal plain development, though many Alaskans outside the energy sector benefit from the refuge staying intact.
The coastal plain is the calving ground of the Porcupine caribou herd the Gwich'in depend on; the designation protects their food supply and culture from industrial development.
